title: Aerobic Respiration
kicker: Cambridge Lower Secondary · Science 0893 · Stage 8 · Biology
summary: How every plant and animal cell releases energy from glucose in its mitochondria, the word equation for aerobic respiration, why it is a controlled release, and the classic experiments — with Checkpoint-style practice.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Know that aerobic respiration happens in the mitochondria of plant and animal cells and gives a controlled release of energy (8Bp.04)
Know and use the word equation for aerobic respiration: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (8Bp.05)

blocks.text: Every living cell needs a constant supply of **energy** — to move, to grow, to keep warm and simply to stay alive. Cells get this energy from **food** (mainly **glucose**) by a chemical reaction called **respiration**. When the reaction uses **oxygen** it is called **aerobic respiration**. It happens in **all living cells**, in plants and in animals, **all the time** — day and night, awake or asleep.

blocks.text: The word equation
**glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water**

headers: Where it comes from / where it goes (humans)
rows: From digested food; carried to cells in the blood **plasma**
From the air in the **lungs**; carried by **red blood cells**
From the air (through the leaves) or from photosynthesis
Carried in the plasma to the lungs and **breathed out**
Used in photosynthesis or released to the air
Used in the body or removed (urine, sweat, breath)
Used in the plant or lost from the leaves

items: Read the arrow as "react to make". Reactants on the **left**, products on the **right**.

**Energy is released**, but energy is **not a substance**, so it is not written as a product. Some books write "(energy released)" next to the arrow — that is fine, but never write "energy" in place of water or carbon dioxide.
The same equation is true for every cell that respires aerobically: muscle cells, root cells, leaf cells, even the cells of your lungs.

blocks.text: **Using symbols (extension, TWSm.03):** scientists write the same reaction with chemical formulae: C_{6}H_{12}O_{6} + 6O_{2} → 6CO_{2} + 6H_{2}O. It shows that **one** glucose molecule reacts with **six** oxygen molecules to make **six** carbon dioxide and **six** water molecules. You must know the **word** equation; the symbol equation is useful but not required.
Where it happens: the mitochondria

Aerobic respiration happens inside tiny structures in the cytoplasm called **mitochondria** (one is a **mitochondrion**). **Both plant and animal cells** have mitochondria. Plant cells also have chloroplasts for photosynthesis, but they still need mitochondria to respire.

blocks.text: Cells that use a lot of energy have **many** mitochondria. For example, **muscle cells** contain far more mitochondria than fat-storage cells, because muscle cells need lots of energy to contract. Root hair cells in plants also have many mitochondria, because they use energy to take in minerals from the soil.
A controlled release of energy

If you burn sugar in a flame, it reacts with oxygen and makes carbon dioxide and water — the same products as respiration. But burning releases **all the energy at once** as **heat and light**, at a very high temperature. That would destroy a cell.

rows: Body temperature — cells are not damaged

blocks.text: **Why a controlled release matters:** the cell can **capture** the energy in small, useful amounts and use it for its jobs, instead of losing it all as heat. Some energy is still released as heat — that is what keeps mammals and birds warm.
What the energy is used for

items: **Movement** — muscle cells contract.
**Growth and repair** — building new cells and making large molecules such as proteins.
**Keeping warm** — mammals and birds keep a steady body temperature (about 37 °C in humans).
**Sending messages** along nerve cells.
**In plants** — growth, and taking in minerals from the soil through root hair cells.

blocks.title: خلاصة التنفس الخلوي
blocks.text: التنفس الخلوي تفاعل كيميائي بيحصل في الميتوكوندريا جوه كل خلية حية — في النبات والحيوان، بالليل والنهار. المعادلة: جلوكوز + أكسجين ← ثاني أكسيد الكربون + ماء. الطاقة بتطلع بالتدريج على خطوات صغيرة (مش مرة واحدة زي الحريق)، عشان الخلية تقدر تستفيد بيها. الطاقة مش مادة، فما بنكتبهاش كناتج في المعادلة.
Respiration, breathing and photosynthesis

rows: Chemical reaction that **releases energy** from glucose
Moving air in and out of the lungs
Chemical reaction that **makes glucose** using light energy

blocks.text: **During exercise** your muscle cells respire faster to release more energy. They need **more oxygen and glucose**, and they make **more carbon dioxide**. So your **breathing rate** and **depth** increase (more oxygen in, more carbon dioxide out) and your **heart rate** increases (blood delivers oxygen and glucose faster and removes carbon dioxide).

items: **Independent variable:** living or dead peas. **Dependent variable:** temperature. **Control variables:** same type and number of peas, same size flask, same starting temperature, same room.
**Why vacuum flasks?** They are insulated, so heat released by respiration is not lost and the rise in temperature can be measured.
**Why disinfect the peas?** To kill microorganisms (bacteria and fungi) on the peas. They also respire and would release heat, so the results would not show the peas' respiration alone.
**Why Flask B?** It is the **control**: it shows that the temperature rise in A is caused by living peas respiring, not by something else.

blocks.text: **2. Respiration produces carbon dioxide.** **Limewater** turns **milky (cloudy)** when carbon dioxide is bubbled through it. Air is drawn through a tube containing small living organisms (for example germinating seeds or maggots resting on gauze), then through limewater. The limewater turns milky. In a **control** tube with glass beads instead of living things, the limewater stays clear. Living animals must be handled carefully and returned to their habitat afterwards.
Worked examples

**Worked example 1** (word equation)
Complete the word equation for aerobic respiration. [2]
glucose + ______ → ______ + water

items: glucose + **oxygen** → **carbon dioxide** + water [1 each]
**Common mistake:** writing "energy" as a product, or writing the photosynthesis equation the wrong way round.

blocks.text:
**Worked example 2** (where respiration happens)
Amina says, "Plants make their food by photosynthesis, so they do not need to respire."
(a) Explain why Amina is wrong. [2]
(b) Name the part of a plant cell where aerobic respiration takes place. [1]

items: (a) All living cells need **energy** (for growth, taking in minerals…) [1]; plants **respire all the time** (day and night) to release energy from the glucose they made [1].
(b) **mitochondria** (accept mitochondrion)
**Common mistake:** "Plants respire only at night." They respire all the time; at night it is just easier to notice because photosynthesis stops.

blocks.text:
**Worked example 3** (the flask experiment)
Use the flask diagram and the graph above.
(a) Calculate the rise in temperature in Flask A over the 5 days. [1]
(b) Explain why the temperature rose in Flask A. [2]
(c) Explain why Flask B was set up. [1]

items: (b) The living peas **respire** [1]; respiration **releases energy**, some of it as **heat**, and the flask stops the heat escaping [1].
(c) It is a **control**, to show the temperature rise is caused by the living (respiring) peas.
**Exam technique:** always read graph values at the exact grid line; here day 5 is halfway between 25 and 26 °C.

blocks.text:
**Worked example 4** (controlled release)
Respiration and burning both turn glucose and oxygen into carbon dioxide and water. Describe one way respiration is different from burning. [1]

items: Respiration releases energy **gradually / in small steps** (a controlled release), but burning releases it **all at once** as heat and light. (Accept: respiration happens at body temperature / inside cells.)
**Common mistake:** "Respiration makes energy." Energy cannot be made — it is **released** from the glucose.

blocks.text:
**Worked example 5** (exercise)
Explain why a runner's breathing rate increases during a race. [3]

items: Her muscle cells need **more energy**, so they carry out **more respiration**. [1]
More respiration needs **more oxygen** (and glucose). [1]
Breathing faster takes in more oxygen and **removes the extra carbon dioxide** made. [1]

blocks.text:
**Worked example 6** (using symbols)
The symbol equation for respiration is C_{6}H_{12}O_{6} + 6O_{2} → 6CO_{2} + 6H_{2}O. How many molecules of oxygen are needed to react with 3 molecules of glucose? [1]

items: 1 glucose needs 6 oxygen, so 3 glucose need 3 × 6 = **18 molecules of oxygen**.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Writing "respiration is breathing". Respiration is a chemical reaction in cells; breathing moves air.
Saying "respiration makes energy" — energy is **released**, not made.
Writing energy as a product in the word equation.
Saying plants only photosynthesise and do not respire, or that they respire only at night.
Saying respiration happens in the nucleus or chloroplasts. Aerobic respiration happens in the **mitochondria**.
Forgetting that respiration is a **controlled** release; burning is not controlled.
In experiments, forgetting to explain the **control** (dead peas / glass beads).

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: **Complete the word equation** — often with one or two gaps. Learn the four words and their order.
**Label a cell** and identify the mitochondria; tick boxes for which cells (plant, animal or both) contain mitochondria.
**Experiments**: germinating seeds and temperature, limewater and carbon dioxide. Expect questions on the control, variables, why disinfect, and reading the graph.
**Explain** links between exercise, respiration, breathing rate and heart rate (3 marks: energy → oxygen → breathing/heart).
**Compare** respiration with burning or with photosynthesis in a table.
Use exact words: **releases** energy, **mitochondria**, **controlled**, **glucose**.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Aerobic respiration: practice
blocks.intro: 14 Checkpoint-style questions, from easy to hard. Check your answers, then read the full solutions.

questions.q: In which part of a cell does aerobic respiration take place?
c: nucleus
cell membrane
chloroplast
mitochondria
questions.e: Aerobic respiration takes place in the mitochondria. Chloroplasts are where photosynthesis happens; the nucleus controls the cell.

questions.q: Complete the word equation: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + ______
Which cells carry out aerobic respiration?
c: the cells of both plants and animals
animal cells only
plant cells only, at night
lung cells only
questions.e: All living plant and animal cells respire all the time, because every cell needs energy. Respiration is not only in the lungs.

questions.q: Name the gas that is used up in aerobic respiration.
questions.e: Oxygen is a reactant: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.

questions.q: Why is aerobic respiration described as a controlled release of energy?
c: It only happens when the body tells it to start
It releases more energy than burning
The energy is released gradually, in many small steps
It releases no heat at all
questions.e: In respiration the energy is released a little at a time, in small steps the cell can use. Burning releases it all at once. Respiration does release some heat, and the total energy is the same as burning the same glucose.

questions.q: (b) Explain why the temperature in Flask B did not change. [2]
questions.ms: 1 mark: the (boiled) peas are dead. 1 mark: so they do not respire / release no energy (heat). Accept: microorganisms were killed by disinfectant, so nothing respired. Do not accept 'the peas were cooked so they were already hot'.
questions.e: Boiling killed the peas, so they could not respire. With no respiration, no energy was released as heat, and the disinfectant had killed the microorganisms, so the temperature stayed at room temperature (20 °C).

questions.q: Which cell is likely to contain the MOST mitochondria?
c: a fat-storage cell
a muscle cell in the leg of an athlete
a cell in the skin of an onion bulb
a cell in the centre of a potato
questions.e: Muscle cells use a great deal of energy to contract, so they need many mitochondria to carry out lots of respiration. The other cells are mainly for storage or covering and use little energy.

questions.q: During exercise, a person's heart rate increases. Use your knowledge of respiration to explain why. [3]
questions.ms: 1 mark: muscles need more energy, so more respiration takes place. 1 mark: so more oxygen and glucose must be delivered to the muscles. 1 mark: and more carbon dioxide must be removed; faster heart rate pumps blood (round the body) faster. Ignore 'the heart needs more energy' alone.
questions.e: The working muscles need more energy, so their cells respire faster. They need more oxygen and glucose delivered, and they make more carbon dioxide that must be removed. The heart beats faster so that blood carries oxygen and glucose to the muscles, and carbon dioxide away, more quickly.

questions.q: Plants make one of the reactants of respiration by photosynthesis. Name this reactant.
questions.e: Photosynthesis makes glucose (and oxygen). The plant uses the glucose in respiration to release energy. (Oxygen is also made in photosynthesis, so 'oxygen' is a reasonable second answer, but glucose is the food reactant.)

questions.q: Which statement about a green plant is correct?
c: It photosynthesises at night and respires during the day
It respires all the time and photosynthesises only in light
It respires only when it is dark
It photosynthesises all the time and never respires
questions.e: Respiration happens in every living cell all the time. Photosynthesis needs light, so it happens only in the light.

questions.q: The symbol equation for aerobic respiration is C_{6}H_{12}O_{6} + 6O_{2} → 6CO_{2} + 6H_{2}O. How many molecules of carbon dioxide are made from 2 molecules of glucose?
questions.e: 1 molecule of glucose makes 6 molecules of carbon dioxide, so 2 molecules make 2 × 6 = 12.

questions.p:
Question 13
Air is drawn through a tube containing maggots and then through limewater. A second tube contains glass beads instead of maggots.
questions.q: (a) Name the gas that makes the limewater turn milky.
questions.e: Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky (cloudy). The maggots release carbon dioxide by respiration.

questions.p:
Question 13
Air is drawn through a tube containing maggots and then through limewater. A second tube contains glass beads instead of maggots.
questions.q: (b) Explain why the tube with glass beads is included. [2]
questions.ms: 1 mark: it is a control. 1 mark: to show that the carbon dioxide (milky limewater) comes from the maggots / living things respiring and not from the air or the apparatus. Accept: glass beads take up the same space but do not respire.
questions.e: The glass beads tube is a control. Glass beads do not respire, so the limewater stays clear (or changes much more slowly). This shows that the extra carbon dioxide in the first tube was made by the maggots' respiration, not by the air or the apparatus.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Aerobic respiration: **glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water** (energy is released, but it is not a product).
It happens in the **mitochondria** of **plant and animal** cells — in every living cell, all the time.
It is a **controlled release** of energy: small steps at body temperature, unlike burning (all at once, as heat and light).
The energy is used for movement, growth and repair, keeping warm and (in plants) taking in minerals.
Evidence: germinating peas warm a vacuum flask; respiring organisms turn limewater milky. Always explain the control.
